passage:
"Mama Yara, a dog chased me!" said Layla at the kitchen table in Amman, arms wide. "It was as big as a bus! And I climbed up a tree, and it went WOOF!"
"As big as a bus!" said Yara. "That is a huge dog. Where was it?"
"By the bakery." Layla thought. "A little bit like a cat."
Yara smiled. "I love this story. Was it a real dog you saw today, or a made-up dog?"
Layla giggled. "Made-up. The real dog was small and sleepy."
"Then it's a wonderful made-up dog," said Yara. "Tell me more."

qa.q: How big did Layla say the dog was?
qa.a: As big as a bus.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling while telling the dog story?
qa.a: Excited and playful, since the arms went wide and the story grew bigger with each sentence.

qa.q: How did Yara enjoy the story and still keep a gentle line on facts?
qa.a: Yara enjoyed the story and then asked, without scolding, whether the dog was real or made-up, and Layla said made-up.

qa.q: How might Yara have felt listening to the bus-sized dog story?
qa.a: Amused and warm, since Yara smiled, said 'I love this story' and asked for more once it was clearly made-up.

grounding: A child tells an exaggerated story about a huge dog, and an adult enjoys it while keeping a gentle line on facts.

passage:
At circle time in the nursery, Gurpreet's hand shot up. "I flew to school this morning on a blanket! Over the road and the cows!"
The children gasped. Ms Jyoti said, "That sounds like a wonderful trip. Was that in your dream, or on the way in the car?"
Gurpreet frowned and thought. "In my dream. But... a little bit real."
"Dream flying is the best flying," said Ms Jyoti. "And this morning the car brought you, with a bus beside it."
"Can I fly again tomorrow, in my dream?" asked Gurpreet.
"You may, and you can tell us."

qa.q: What did Gurpreet say was used for flying to school?
qa.a: A blanket.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling while sharing the flying story, and what does the frown suggest?
qa.a: Excited, and for a moment unsure whether it was real, since the frown and "a little bit real" show dream and fact were still blurred.

qa.q: What did Ms Jyoti do that respected the story and the facts?
qa.a: Ms Jyoti praised the trip, asked whether it was a dream or the car, and named how Gurpreet really came to school.

qa.q: How might the other children feel about Gurpreet's flying story?
qa.a: Amazed and curious, since they gasped when they heard it and may want to share dreams of their own.

grounding: A child tells an exaggerated flying story that blurs dream and fact, and an adult enjoys it while gently keeping a line on facts.

passage:
Monday: Deepak, five, ran in from the colony gate. "Mummy! I saw a dog as big as a bus! It had three tails!" Neelam laughed. "Three tails! What colour?" "Purple!" "Wow, what a story!"
Wednesday: At dinner, Deepak said, "I flew to school today. Over the trees." Neelam smiled. "Was that in your dream or for real?" Deepak thought. "Dream. But it felt real!" "Dreams can feel very real."
Saturday: Deepak said, "I saw a big dog." Then he added, "A pretend one, a bus dog!" Neelam hugged him, laughing. "I love your pretend dogs."

qa.q: How many tails did Deepak say the dog had?
qa.a: Three tails.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel telling his tall tales?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud of his imaginative stories.

qa.q: How did Neelam keep a gentle line on facts?
qa.a: She enjoyed the stories but asked 'Was that in your dream or for real?', helping Deepak separate pretend from real.

qa.q: What changed in Deepak by Saturday?
qa.a: He started labelling his own tall tale as 'a pretend one' without being asked.

grounding: Shows a child telling exaggerated tales and a parent enjoying them while gently separating pretend from real.

passage: During the power cut at the preschool, the fans stopped, and Neelam ma'am gathered the children in the corridor with a torch for story time. Rukmini, five, put her hand up. "I saw a tiger in my garden! It was THIS big!" She spread her arms. "It ate my slipper!" The children gasped. Neelam ma'am smiled. "A tiger! That's a big story. Was it a real tiger or a pretend tiger?" Rukmini thought. "Pretend. But it was hungry." Everyone laughed. "Pretend tigers get very hungry," Neelam ma'am said. "Shall we make up more of its story?" The class spent the power cut deciding what the tiger ate next.

qa.q: What did Rukmini say the tiger ate?
qa.a: Her slipper.

qa.q: How did Rukmini seem to feel telling the tiger story?
qa.a: She seemed excited and proud, spreading her arms to show its size.

qa.q: What did Neelam ma'am do that respected both imagination and facts?
qa.a: She enjoyed the story but asked if it was real or pretend, then turned it into a shared make-believe game.

qa.q: How did the other children respond to Rukmini's story?
qa.a: They gasped and then laughed, joining in to invent more of the tiger's story.

grounding: Shows a child telling a tall tale and an adult enjoying it while gently marking the line between pretend and real.

passage: At the colony pool in Chennai, Jaya, six, climbed out dripping and ran to her big sister Aditi. "Akka! I swam with a whale! A real whale! It had a hat!" Aditi raised her eyebrows. "A whale in the colony pool?" "Yes! It said hello!" Aditi laughed. "That's an amazing story. Was it real, or a pretend whale?" Jaya giggled. "Pretend. But it had a hat." "The best whales have hats," Aditi said. "Tell me what colour the hat was." Jaya told her, all the way home.

qa.q: What did Jaya say the whale had?
qa.a: A hat.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel telling her whale story?
qa.a: She felt excited and happy, giggling as she told it.

qa.q: How did Aditi keep a gentle line on facts?
qa.a: She asked if it was real or pretend, then kept enjoying the story, asking about the hat.

qa.q: What would change if Aditi had called it a lie?
qa.a: Jaya might have felt ashamed and stopped sharing her imaginative stories.

grounding: Shows a child telling a tall tale and an older sister enjoying it while gently marking what is pretend.

passage:
"Papa! A dog chased me today. It was as big as a bus!"
"As big as a bus?" Kamal put down his newspaper. "Did it have wheels?"
"No! It had six legs and red eyes!"
"Wow. What did you do?"
"I flew! Up to the water tank."
Kamal laughed. "Brilliant story. Now tell me the true part. Was there a real dog?"
Charu twisted her frock. "A brown dog by the gate. It barked. I ran to Dadi."
"Good thing you ran to Dadi. And the flying?"
"...That was a story part."
"Best story part," Kamal said. "Draw me the six-legged one?"

qa.q: Where did Charu run when the brown dog barked?
qa.a: She ran to Dadi.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling when the real dog barked?
qa.a: She was probably scared, which may be why her story made the dog huge and let her fly away.

qa.q: How did Kamal keep a gentle line on the facts?
qa.a: He enjoyed the story, then asked for "the true part", so Charu could tell what really happened without being called a liar.

qa.q: How did Kamal seem to feel about Charu's tall tale?
qa.a: He seemed amused and delighted, calling it a brilliant story and asking for a drawing.

grounding: Shows a young child telling a tall tale about a huge dog and a parent enjoying it while gently asking for the true part.
